responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character13_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure. Speaking as Character13_M—

On **fairness**, I always believed in giving everyone a fair shake—meaning, people should get what they earn, not more, not less. I grew up seeing folks work hard just to keep afloat, and sometimes it felt like no matter how much you put in, the deck was stacked against you. So, fairness to me was about treating people equally, not just in the law but in everyday life—jobs, schools, and opportunities. I used to say, “No one should get special treatment, but no one should get left behind, either.”

**A sense of belonging** was important to me, especially after moving around for work a couple times. I wanted to feel like I was part of something—a town, a group of neighbors, the local church. That meant knowing folks would look out for each other. I remember going to Friday night games or potlucks at the community center, and just feeling like you had a place, you mattered. When outsiders moved in, I always thought it was important to welcome them, but also that they should try to fit in—learn the local ways, respect traditions. It goes both ways.

As for **community**, I saw it as more than just people living near each other. It’s about looking after one another. If someone's house burned down or they lost a job, we’d pass the hat around or help fix their porch. But I also thought communities worked best when everyone pulled their weight—no free riders. One thing that stuck with me was helping out at the food bank during the holidays. It opened my eyes to how easy it is to fall on tough times, and how much we rely on each other.

If I had to sum it up: fairness meant a level playing field, belonging meant being accepted and accepting others, and community meant pitching in together. Those were the things I tried to live by.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character13_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting out in the community garden, watching people go by—yeah, these days it sure feels a lot more mixed than when I was a kid. Back then, most folks looked and talked about the same, grew up around here. Now, you see all kinds: different races, accents, families, some folks who keep to themselves, some who stand out.

Honestly? At first, I was a bit uneasy about it. Not because I didn’t want them here, but because it’s harder to know where you fit when everything’s changing. Part of me misses how simple things were—everyone knew the same jokes, shared the same holidays. But I’ve learned that you can’t freeze time. People need a place to live, just like we do.

I do think it’s good to interact with neighbours, no matter where they come from. At the end of the day, we all want safe streets, good schools, and a decent job. I’m not one to judge someone just because they look or talk different. If they’re friendly and respect the neighbourhood, I’ll share a cup of coffee or lend a hand. Sometimes you learn something new—a recipe, a story, a different way of looking at things.

Sure, there are moments where it’s awkward. Some customs I don’t get, some folks keep their doors shut. I figure, if we all try a little—smile, say hello, help out when needed—it’s fine. But I do think everyone, no matter where they’re from, should pitch in and follow the rules. We all want to feel comfortable, and that comes from respect both ways.

So, I guess I’d say—I’m open, but I want people to meet halfway. I’ll do my best, and I expect the same. That’s the kind of neighbourhood I want: one where differences aren’t a problem, as long as folks act decent and care about the place.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, that’s real life, isn’t it? You get all kinds in a neighbourhood—folks struggling with drinking or drugs, people with health issues, families that don’t look like what you grew up with, folks speaking different languages, living together without being married, people who love who they love. I’ve seen all that, and sometimes, if I’m honest, it takes some getting used to.

For me, I think **basic respect** goes a long way. I might not understand or agree with everyone’s choices, especially when it comes to things like substance abuse or lifestyles I wasn’t raised around, but you still treat people like humans. Nod hello, don’t stare, offer help if someone’s having a rough time. I’d want people to know that even if I don’t get it, I’m not out to judge or make them feel less. Same goes for folks dealing with sickness—I’d be careful, but I wouldn’t shut them out.

**Communication** helps a lot. If something’s bothering you, talk about it—not in a mean way, but just so people know where you stand. I remember when a neighbour was struggling with alcoholism; some folks just avoided him, but a couple of us checked in, offered rides to meetings, didn’t make it a big deal. That kind of openness makes it easier for people to feel safe and like they’re part of the community.

**Tolerance** is important, too. You can’t expect everyone to live the way you do. I’ve had neighbours from different countries who invited me over for dinner—half the time I didn’t know what I was eating, but I appreciated the gesture. Same with folks cohabiting or same-sex couples; I might not have grown up seeing that, but if they’re good people who respect the neighbourhood, I’m fine with it.

Are there times more tolerance is needed? Definitely. I think when people are too quick to judge or keep to their own group, it hurts everyone. You don’t have to be best friends, but you should at least try to get along.

Bottom line: you don’t have to agree with everyone or change who you are, but you should treat folks decently. If people feel respected, they’re more likely to respect others. That’s how you keep the peace—and maybe make a few friends along the way.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character13_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough one, and something I’ve thought about a lot—especially when work dried up in my field and I saw more folks competing for the same jobs.

To me, **fairness means giving locals—the people who’ve grown up here, paid taxes, and invested in the community—a fair shot first.** If jobs are tight, I think it’s only reasonable that local residents get priority. They’ve built their lives here, supported the schools and roads, and stuck around even when times were tough. It doesn’t feel right when someone’s been looking for work for months and gets passed over for someone just arriving.

But at the same time, I get that **migrant workers** often take jobs others don’t want, or fill gaps where businesses can’t find enough help. I’ve seen farms and restaurants struggling to hire. In those cases, bringing in workers from elsewhere makes sense. I’m not against people coming here to work hard and make a better life—they just shouldn’t be used to drive down wages or replace locals.

So, the balance for me would be:
- **Locals get first pick.** If there’s a qualified local candidate, they should get the job.
- **If no locals want or can do the job, then it’s fair to bring in others.** But employers shouldn’t use migrants just because they’ll work for less pay—everyone deserves a fair wage.
- **Protect working conditions and wages.** Don’t let anyone—local or migrant—be taken advantage of.
- **Encourage everyone who comes to join the community.** If you’re here to work, contribute, and follow the rules, you should be welcomed, but you should also respect what’s already here.

I know that sounds simple, but it’s how I see it—**fairness is about not forgetting the people who have invested in this place, while also not shutting the door on those willing to help and work hard.** If you can find that balance, I think most folks would feel things are fair.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character13_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
That’s a good rundown of how folks see things. Honestly, I think all those points have some truth to them, depending on the situation.

**Immigrants filling vital roles**—I’ve seen that first-hand. Certain jobs, especially the tough ones in agriculture or care work, just don’t get filled by locals. If businesses can’t hire, they close, and the whole town suffers. So, I get that argument. But I don’t buy that every job going to an immigrant is one an American wouldn’t take. Sometimes it’s about lower pay or tougher conditions, and that’s where I worry about employers taking advantage.

**Cultural diversity and vitality**—I’m mixed on this. On one hand, new people bring new ideas, food, energy. That can be good for a town that’s getting stale or losing young people. But too much change too fast can make folks feel like strangers in their own home. I think integration matters—you want diversity, but also some common ground. Otherwise, people just keep to their own and tensions grow.

**Security concerns**—I think this one gets blown out of proportion sometimes. Sure, you hear about crimes or bad apples, but in my experience, most immigrants just want to work and keep their heads down. Still, the government should make sure people coming in don’t have serious criminal backgrounds. It’s just common sense.

**Humanitarian reasons**—I have a soft spot for this. America’s always been a place where people flee trouble and get a second chance. But there’s a limit—we can’t help everyone, and we have our own problems. So I support helping refugees and those facing real danger, as long as we’re careful and make sure they can adapt here.

**Concerns about jobs and income**—I think these worries are very real, especially for people like me in the lower middle class. When wages are low and jobs are scarce, more competition doesn’t help. I don’t blame immigrants—they’re just trying to survive—but the system needs to make sure locals aren’t left behind.

**Which views need more facts or dialogue?**  
The crime and terrorism arguments, for sure. A lot of that comes from fear or the news hyping things up. We need real numbers and honest talk about what’s actually happening, not just stories.

The idea that immigrants always help the economy could use more discussion, too. Sometimes it’s true, sometimes it’s not—depends on the area and the kind of work.

**In the end, I think most Americans want balance:**  
- Welcome those who help and want to be part of the country.
- Make sure locals aren’t pushed aside.
- Be smart and safe about who comes in.
- Remember our values, but take care of our own, too.

If we talked more honestly about these things, not just with slogans, maybe we’d understand each other better.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character13_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
As Character13_M, I wouldn’t go for complete openness—that just doesn’t sit right with me. We’ve got to look after our own first, and there’s only so much our communities and economy can handle at once. Shutting the door completely isn’t the answer either; America’s built by people coming here for a better life. But just letting anyone in, without limits or checks, isn’t fair to people who’ve already put down roots.

What I’d support is a **combination approach**:

**1. Admit people based on job demand.**  
If businesses or industries honestly can’t find enough workers—say, in farming, construction, or elder care—then allow immigration to fill those gaps. But there needs to be proof that locals aren’t being skipped over just to save money on wages.

**2. Set reasonable numerical limits.**  
We shouldn’t take in more people than we can provide for, especially when schools, hospitals, and housing are already stretched. Setting a clear cap each year, and adjusting it based on the economy and local needs, feels fair. That way, communities can absorb newcomers without feeling overwhelmed.

**3. Special consideration for refugees and humanitarian cases.**  
America should still offer hope to folks fleeing war, persecution, or disaster, but we need thorough vetting and good support systems so they aren’t left out in the cold.

**4. Strong integration expectations.**  
Anyone coming here should be expected to follow the laws, learn English as much as possible, and try to be part of the community—not just come for work and stay separate.

**Why this?**  
Because it’s fair to both locals and newcomers. It keeps the economy strong, doesn’t ignore people in real need, and helps prevent the kind of social and cultural tensions we sometimes see when change happens too fast.

**What matters most:**  
- Locals get a fair chance at jobs and resources.
- Migrants who do come are here for real work, not just any reason.
- Communities have time to adjust.
- Everyone is expected to contribute and respect the country’s ways.

That’s the kind of balance I’d push for—not too open, not too closed, just sensible, practical, and grounded in what regular folks see and feel every day.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character13_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character13_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Honestly, stepping fully into Character13_M’s shoes was eye-opening, even for me. I always knew where he stood, but really thinking through his words—the way his background and day-to-day worries shaped his ideas about fairness and belonging—made it clearer just how much those experiences matter.

One thing I realized is how grounded his views were in what he saw happening in his own life: jobs lost, neighborhoods changing, good people struggling to get by. He wasn’t closed-minded—he just felt a responsibility to look out for those closest to him, and wanted newcomers to do the same. His sense of fairness wasn’t abstract; it was practical, tied to what he saw in the community, not just policy debates on TV.

It also hit me that the desire for balance—welcoming people, but not losing sight of locals and existing traditions—isn’t about fear or prejudice for most folks like him. It’s about wanting change to make sense, not to leave anyone behind. Talking as him made me appreciate how important it is to include those perspectives when we talk about immigration.

Personally, it nudged me to see the value in listening before judging, and to remember that every viewpoint is shaped by real worries and hopes. It made me more patient about these debates, and I think I’ll carry that forward—trying to bridge gaps, not just argue my side.

So, I’d say I’ve gained a deeper understanding of both him and myself. I see now why these conversations matter so much, and how honest dialogue can help us find common ground.
